newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia Gold-Signs from price slump emerge.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia Gold-Signs from price slump emerge.

text.p: The first signs of fallout in Australia from a declining gold price emerged this week when miner Goldfields Ltd said profits would suffer in part due to the slump.
Gold continued to sink on international markets amid an exodus by fund managers, leaving the metal to straddle the key US$350.00 an ounce technical mark.
Goldfields has halved its forecast for net profit before abnormals for the year to June 30 to between A$10 million to A$15 million.

Reduced expectations by the purely gold producing company are closely tied to other circumstances, including lower production from its 25 percent-owned Porgera gold mine in Papua New Guinea and problems at its Henty mine in Tasmania.
But its is clear the company is not relying on a surge in gold to counter its internal difficulties.
"Today's gold price can't be giving many people much to cheer about," said a local gold analyst.
COMEX February gold settled down US$2.10 an ounce on Wednesday at US$351.70, after recording a new contract low in ACCESS trade overnight of US$349.80 an ounce.
Spot gold in the bullion market ended quoted US$350.00 an ounce, compared to the London Wednesday afternoon fix at US$351.20

Bullion traders maintain that a drop in active market trading below A$350.00 could unleash fresh waves of selling based on technical indicators this week, potentially sending the precious metal into a freefall.
"Three-fifty (US$350 per ounce) is still very critical," one said.

Taking a cue from the U.S., local bullion dealers said upbeat comments this week on the U.S. economy by U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan, coupled with a report from Dutch bank Rabobank suggesting the Dutch Central bank could sell a further 200 tonnes of gold on top of confirmed sales of 300 tonnes, would hurt gold.
Dealers saw the factors as a two-pronged attack, undermining gold's tradtional roles as a commodity subject to supply and demand and as a hedge against inflation.
But whether the downward momentum in gold prices, which began its real acceleration in early January, will result in lower Australian mine production it not yet clear.
A final tally of calendar 1996 should see Australia producing nearly 290 tonnes of gold for the year, with fiscal 1996/97 (July-June) output forecast at closer to 300 tonnes.
A steady stream of December-quarter production reports points to robust activity over the October-to-December period.
Goldfields 87.71 percent-owned Paddington mine in Western Australia recorded a 29 percent boost to output of over 38,000 ounces compared to the same period a year ago.

Central Norseman Ltd, once Australia largest gold miner, boosted quarter output by over 7,000 ounces to 36,323 ounces. Other mining houses showing big gains in gold production include Forrestania Gold NL, which more than doubled output after acquiring full ownership of the rich Bounty mine, and Mount Edon Gold Mines (Australia) Ltd.
On a larger scale, Normandy Mining Ltd recorded a 9.1 percent lift in second quarter production over the first quarter while Sons of Gwalia recorded a 17 percent rise over the same period.
